title: Ian Pryce inquest makes recommendations
subtitle: Police should investigate when given a name by a person they have contained, among inquest recommendations.
article: Minutes before he died, Ian Pryce told police to call his friend Sherry-Ann Lotz. They didn't , and Pryce was killed.
Now, a coroner's inquest looking into the shooting deaths of Ian Pryce has recommended police should investigate when given a name by a person contained by police, the way Pryce did.

The inquest also recommended police immediately seek the assistance of a mental health professional when dealing with a person undergoing a mental health crisis, and recommended regulating the possession of replica firearms.

The jury in the inquest delivered the recommendations Thursday afternoon, after three weeks of testimony on what exactly happened in November 2013 when Pryce was shot and killed by two police officers after a tense standoff on Sherbourne St.
On Wednesday, members of Pryce's family, as well as representatives from the Toronto Police Services Board, presented what they thought should be included in the recommendations.

Among those that made it into the final recommendations were those by Heather Thompson, Pryce's mother, asking for police to investigate when given a name by a person in containment, and to get assistance from a mental health professional.
Thompson also requested a study on the feasibility of recording negotiations between police officers and those contained by police, which the jury recommended.
Out of the police's proposals, the regulation of replica firearms, and firearms that fire projectiles at less than 500 feet a second made it into the final recommendations.
Pryce, who had been living with paranoid schizophrenia, was armed with what police initially believed was a pistol, but turned out to be a pellet gun.

A separate proposal by the chief of the Toronto Police Service to require dispatchers to notify officers when someone calls to say they're in the location of an incident didn't make it into the jury's recommendations, but was already put into policy by Toronto Police.

The inquest was called not to assign blame for Pryce's death, but to examine the circumstances around it. The five-member jury was also told not to make recommendations on the mental health systems, but to limit them to improvements to police actions.

A Special Investigations Unit investigation cleared, but didn't name, the two officers who shot Pryce. Their names became known during the course of the coroner's inquest. Const. Thomas Mackenzie, who fired the shot that killed Pryce, and Sgt. Robert Monteiro, whose shot hit Pryce in the eye but didn't kill him, both testified they believed Pryce posed an imminent threat to the police officers and possible bystanders nearby.
"I had made the decision he was going to shoot someone or injure someone," Monteiro said.

Pryce's sister, Carrie Pryce, told the Star she had mixed feelings about the recommendations. She was happy with some of the recommendations but said she felt the inquest was stacked against the family from the beginning. When asked whether she hoped the recommendations would change anything, Pryce was pessimistic.
"The changes will not occur with this inquest, where you have six lawyers representing police and two representing the family," Pryce said.

Heather Thompson, Pryce's mother, said the inquest process has been an extremely difficult experience, particularly listening to the audio of the negotiations with police. Hearing the sounds of gunshots "was gut-wrenching," she said. "The moment the two shots hit my son was horrific."
She's hopeful the recommendations will help prevent another tragedy, "because there are many sick people in this city."
"These recommendations will hopefully save another mom from going through this," she said.
But Thompson can't help feeling regret that these measures were not already in place. "They could have saved his life," she said.
While Thompson says she now knows more about the circumstances that led to her son's death, her ordeal is far from over.
"I am a mom who does not have a son," she said, "And I know Ian did not want to die, and he did not want to hurt anybody."
Thompson was represented by Toronto lawyer Peter Rosenthal, while Pryce's sisters were represented separately.
Rosenthal said he was very happy with the recommendations, pointing out the same provisions as Carrie Pryce on how police handle people in mental health crisis and contacting third parties.
"In this case, that would have probably saved Mr. Pryce ... If they had contacted Sherry-Ann, they would have have found out ... that she could have been an enormous help," Rosenthal said.
Carrie Pryce said she also believes Pryce's death could have been prevented.
"I know he could have been saved."
